text:
I was confused why I came, and I was still confused when I was standing at the gate. Three months now since my grandma left. The garden is feral. Morning glories are all over the rusted trellis, climbing it, they look like little blue hands. Her roses have thrown out canes all over, thorny and unrepentant. Knee-high grass around the birdbath. There was a robin in there, bathing, as if nothing has changed. I had my keys and a paper bag of groceries. House is empty, sold to young couple. They wanted to renovate. They gave me till Sunday to take what I want. What I want isn't in the house. It's out here. In the damp earth and the smell of tomato leaves. In the crooked row of lavender she insisted grew better when you ignored it.
She taught me to garden the summer I turned nine. After my parents divorced. She said you don't yank the roots, you ask the soil for what you need, gently. She was kneeling next to me, hands spotted and sure. Straw hat with the torn brim, man's denim shirt. Smelled like sunscreen and mint. I remember thinking she was the oldest thing in the world, and the kindest.
She lives in a memory care unit now, forty minutes away. Hall smells like disinfectant and lemon cake. She doesn't recognize me much. Last week I went and she looked past me, out the window, and said the tomatoes need staking. I said they do. She said use the twine in the shed. Not the green one, the brown. I said I will. She nodded, satisfied, closed her eyes. And she was gone for a moment again.
I put the groceries on the porch, walked into the garden. Gate creaks like an old man. Inside it's thick, green, humid cathedral of leaves. Peony bushes collapsed under their own blooms, petals browning at the edges. The stone path she laid herself, one flat rock at a time, is barely visible under creeping thyme. I knelt, pulled a handful of weeds. Soil cool, loose, alive with worms.
Voice behind me. You're going to get your hands dirty. I turned. Mrs. Alvarez, the neighbor, stood at the fence with a trowel. She's been there forty years. Shared tomatoes and gossip with grandma, once a bottle of whiskey on New Year's Eve. I said I don't mind. She said she'd be glad someone was tending it. She used to say a garden is a conversation, if you stop talking it forgets you. I laughed, but it came out like a cough. She's forgetting a lot these days. Her face softened. Not this. Not the garden. She asks about it every time I visit. Wants to know if the figs are ripe. I said they aren't, not yet. She said then you'll have to tell her when they are.
She went back to her yard, I was alone. Worked without gloves, pulled weeds till my nails were black. Found the twine in the shed, brown and frayed, tied the tomatoes to their stakes. Leaves smell sharp and green, like my grandma's hands. I talked to the plants, softly, the way she did. There. There you go.
By late afternoon sun had shifted, garden looked less wild. Not restored, that takes seasons, but acknowledged. Roses still sprawled, but I cut back the worst of the canes. Lavender stood in its crooked row, forgiving. I sat on the stone bench by the birdbath, watched a bee stumble into a foxglove. Light was gold and slanted, the way it is before evening, everything seems briefly possible.
Phone buzzed. Memory care. I answered. Hello. Miss, a nurse's voice, gentle. Your grandmother is asking for you. Says she wants to tell you something about the garden. Throat tightened. I said I'll be there in forty. Drove with the windows down, cut grass and exhaust. Arrived, she was in a chair by the window, blanket over her knees. She looked smaller than I remembered, like a bird in winter.
She said you came. I said I did. She reached for my hand, her fingers were cold, but her grip was surprisingly strong. She said the tomatoes. I said I staked them, with the brown twine. She smiled, slow, distant. Good girl. And the figs? I said not yet. She said they'll come, you have to wait. I nodded. We sat in silence, watching light fade through blinds. Parking lot outside was gray and ordinary, but in my mind I saw the garden, green and breathing, tomatoes leaning toward the sun. I squeezed her hand, she squeezed back. For a moment we were both in the same place. Then her eyes drifted closed, and I stayed, holding on, until the nurse came to say it was time to go.
Drove home in the dark. When I got to the house, I stood at the gate, listened. Crickets loud. Garden quiet. But it was still there, waiting.
